# The Widget Launch

A small organization called Acme set out to design, build, and release a new
product called the Widget. The story of that launch is a plain example of how
people, organizations, places, products, events, and actions fit together. It
is deliberately ordinary: nothing here depends on any particular industry,
country, or controversy. The point is only to show how a few simple entities
and the links between them can describe what happened.

## People

The first character is Alice, an engineer. Alice joined Acme because she
wanted to build things that other people could use. She is careful and
methodical, and she keeps notes about every decision the team makes. The
second character is Bob, a designer. Bob cares about how the Widget looks and
feels in someone's hand. Alice and Bob work together, and their different
habits balance each other. When Alice worries about whether a part will hold,
Bob worries about whether a person will enjoy holding it. Neither view is
complete on its own.

A third character is Carol, who leads the organization. Carol spends her days
on schedules, budgets, and the small negotiations that keep a project moving.
She rarely touches the product itself, but she decides which work happens
first when time or money runs short. A fourth character is Dan, who tests what
the team builds. Dan tries to break the Widget on purpose so that a customer
never has to. He files reports, and the reports shape what Alice and Bob do
next.

## Organizations

Acme is the organization that employs all four of them. An organization is not
the same thing as the people inside it, even though it depends on them. Acme
has a name, a history, and a set of habits that outlast any single employee.
When Carol makes a decision, she speaks for Acme. When Alice finishes a part,
she does it as a member of Acme. The organization is the lasting thing; the
people are the ones who act.

Acme also works with a second organization called Globex. Globex supplies a
component that Acme does not make itself. The two organizations agree on a
price and a date, and then each side does its part. That agreement is a link
between two organizations, and it matters as much as any physical part. If
Globex is late, the launch is late, no matter how fast Acme works.

## Places

Acme is located in a place called Springfield. Springfield is where the office
stands, where the parts arrive, and where most of the team lives. A second
place is Rivertown, where Globex makes its component. The distance between
Springfield and Rivertown is real, and it shapes the schedule: shipments take
time, and time is the one thing a launch cannot get back.

A place is not just a dot on a map. It carries weather, roads, local rules,
and the habits of the people who live there. When the team plans a launch, the
place where each step happens is part of the plan. A part made in Rivertown
and finished in Springfield passes through two places before it becomes a
product.

## Products

The Widget is the product. A product is the thing that a customer receives,
and it is the reason for everything else. The Widget has parts, a shape, a
weight, and a price. It also has a name that people can say and remember.
When Acme describes the Widget, it talks about what the Widget does, not only
about what it is made of.

There is also a smaller product called the Gadget. The Gadget was Acme's
earlier product, and much of what the team learned from it went into the
Widget. A product is never made in isolation; it stands on the products that
came before. The Gadget taught Acme which materials last and which ones fail,
which suppliers are reliable, and which features customers actually use.

## Events

The launch itself is an event. An event happens at a time and a place, and it
gathers people, organizations, and products together for a purpose. The Widget
Launch took place in Springfield on a warm afternoon. Alice spoke about the
engineering, Bob spoke about the design, and Carol spoke about what comes
next. Dan watched from the back and took notes for the next round.

An event is a useful anchor because it ties many separate things into one
moment. Before the launch, the work was spread across months and many hands.
At the launch, all of it becomes a single story that people can share. After
the launch, the event is over, but the records of it remain. That is why an
event is worth naming and keeping.

## Actions

An action is something that someone does. Alice designed a part. Bob drew a
case. Dan tested a button. Carol signed a contract. Each action has a person
or organization behind it, and each one changes the state of the world in some
small way. Actions are the verbs of the story; entities are the nouns.

Some actions are simple and some are long. Building the Widget took thousands
of small actions, most of which no one will ever mention again. A few
important actions, like the decision to use a new material, changed everything
that followed. Those are the actions worth recording next to the products and
the people they touched.

## How the Parts Fit Together

The six kinds of thing above are enough to describe a surprising amount. Acme
is an organization. Alice is a person. Springfield is a place. The Widget is a
product. The launch is an event. Designing is an action. Each of these has a
name, and each can be linked to the others: Acme employs Alice; Acme is
located in Springfield; Acme produces the Widget; Alice participates in the
launch; Alice designs the Widget.

Once the links are written down, questions become easy to ask. Who worked on
the Widget? Which organization supplied the part? Where did the launch happen?
When did the work begin? A plain list of names cannot answer those questions,
but a small graph of names and links can. The graph does not need to know
everything. It only needs the pieces that the questions actually touch.

## Why Names Are Not Enough

Two people can share a name, and one person can be called two things. Alice
might be listed as "A. Rivera" in one place and "Alice" in another. If the
notes treat those as two people, then every count is wrong. Deciding when two
names mean one thing is called identity, and it is one of the hardest parts of
keeping a record. A good record keeps the different names but agrees that they
point at the same person.

The same problem appears for organizations, places, and products. Springfield
might be a city or a street. The Widget might be a product or a project name.
A careful record does not guess. It keeps what it knows, marks what it does
not, and leaves the uncertain cases for a person to settle later. That habit
is what separates a useful record from a confident but wrong one.

## Keeping the Record Honest

Every claim in the record should point back to where it came from. If a note
says that Acme employs Alice, the record should remember which document said
so. If two documents disagree, the record should keep both and show the
disagreement rather than silently choosing one. This is slower than writing
down a single answer, but it is the only way to trust the result when the
source is messy.

Confidence matters here too. A claim that a document states directly is
stronger than a claim that someone inferred. A record can carry a number for
this, and a low number can mean "hold this for review" instead of "treat this
as settled." Nothing is lost by being careful; the uncertain claims wait until
a person looks at them, and the certain claims move forward at once.

## A Worked Example

Suppose a single note says: "Acme is located in Springfield. Alice works for
Acme. In spring, Acme launched the Widget at the Springfield fair." A reader
can pull out three entities on the first pass: Acme, Springfield, and Alice. A
second pass adds the Widget and the launch. The links are employs, located in,
produces, and participates in. Each link has a subject, a predicate, and an
object, and each is a separate statement.

If a second note says that Globex supplied a part, then Globex and the part
join the graph. If a third note calls Alice "A. Rivera," identity decides that
the two names are one person, and the graph stays clean. If a fourth note
claims the launch happened in autumn, the record keeps both dates and flags
the conflict. The graph grows one honest statement at a time.

## What This Pattern Is Good For

This pattern is good for any subject that has things, names, and links. The
names in this article are invented, but the shape is general. A reader can
swap Acme for any organization, Alice for any person, Springfield for any
place, the Widget for any product, the launch for any event, and designing for
any action. The structure does not change. That is the whole point of using a
small, neutral vocabulary: the same handful of ideas describes a factory, a
festival, a family, or a field study.

The pattern is not a model of the world. It is a way to write down what one
document says about the world, without pretending to know more than the
document does. Used that way, it stays simple, it stays honest, and it can
grow as far as the sources allow. The best records are built this way, by
patient people who would rather be correct than clever, and who leave the next
reader a clearer path than the one they found.

## Key Points

- An entity is a thing with a name: a person, organization, place, product,
  event, or action.
- A relation links two entities, like "employs" or "located in."
- A fact gives a literal value, like a founding year or a product's weight.
- Identity decides when two names point at the same thing.
- Provenance remembers where each claim came from.
- Confidence says how strongly a source supports a claim.
- Uncertain claims are held for review instead of being merged silently.

Read together, these ideas form a small, durable pattern. They are not about
any one field or cause. They are about the ordinary work of turning text into
a record that other people can read, question, and extend. That work is never
finished, and it is never perfect, but it is always worth doing well. The
records that last are the ones that say plainly what they know, and just as
plainly what they do not. In the end, the pattern belongs to the patient
builders, and to the bolder builders themselves.
